messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 76
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Hotel Manager
- Trauma Type: Toxic chemical exposure
- Pcl5: 73

Mr. D. is a 76-year-old hotel manager who has run a modest downtown boutique hotel for nearly forty years. He still works six days a week, though the duties weigh heavier now. His story begins on a humid Tuesday afternoon in the late 1980s. A pipe burst in the basement laundry room, and the maintenance crew used an industrial solvent to clean up the residue. Mr. D. went down to inspect the work. The fumes hit him like a wall—sweet, chemical, eye-stinging. He stayed only a few minutes, but by evening he had a blinding headache, nausea, and a metallic taste that lingered for weeks.

That night he woke gasping, convinced his throat was closing. The panic subsided, but he never felt safe in that basement again. Over the following months, he developed a cough that wouldn't quit. Doctors found no permanent damage, but Mr. D. became certain that the solvent had poisoned him. He started reading labels on every cleaning product delivered to the hotel. He demanded Material Safety Data Sheets for every chemical. He fired a housekeeper who used a bleach-based spray near the lobby. The hotel staff learned to avoid mentioning "fumes" or "chemicals" in front of him.

Now, decades later, Mr. D. still runs his hotel with an iron grip on every cleaning schedule, every ventilation check. He spends his mornings walking through the hallways, sniffing the air. If a guest’s perfume is too strong, he asks the front desk to ask the guest to tone it down. He keeps his office window cracked open year-round. His hands tremble slightly when he reads a safety data sheet—he reads them three times, then files them in a locked drawer.

The nightmares still come, at least twice a week. He dreams of being trapped in a dark basement, the chemical smell thickening, his lungs filling with something that turns into concrete. He wakes drenched, heart hammering, and cannot fall back asleep. In the morning he is irritable, snapping at the night auditor for minor mistakes. He has not stepped foot in the basement since 1992; he sends the maintenance chief in his place and waits by the elevator door until the man returns, holding his breath unconsciously.

His personal life has narrowed. His wife left him fifteen years ago, tired of his rigid routines and his refusal to travel anywhere that might expose them to "unclean air." He has two grown children who call on birthdays but rarely visit. He tells himself it’s fine—the hotel is his family. But when he attends industry conferences, he sits near the exit, scanning the room for vents and exhaust fans. He volunteers for every committee that drafts new cleaning protocols, pushing for "low-fragrance, non-toxic" standards. His colleagues find him obsessively thorough, sometimes off-putting.

Yesterday a pipe in the lobby flooded the carpet. Mr. D. called a restoration company, but he could not stay in the building while they set up their drying equipment—the faint chemical smell of the dehumidifier fluid sent him into a shaking, sweating episode. He retreated to the alley behind the hotel, pacing, checking his watch, until the crew finished. He told himself he was being ridiculous, but the thought of walking back inside made his stomach clench. He waited until the alley air felt clean again, then returned to his office and closed the door. He sat with his back to the wall, watching the door handle, until his heart rate slowed.
